data.name: Sometimes Always Monsters
data.detailed_description:
Sometimes Always Monsters is a narrative roleplaying life simulator filled with choices.

You play a recently married author who joins a cross-country bus tour to promote your next upcoming novel. Along the way, you hear about vicious rumours claiming you're a total fraud.

As you journey through five unique cities, meet fans and critics alike, and make friends with your fellow busmates, it'll be your choices that help unravel the conspiracy laid against you.

Roleplay Creatively as you navigate the life of your character. In addition to countless dialogue choices, you'll decide how you want to live. Whether you like being a diligent workaholic, or prefer the route of a relaxed layabout, the choice is entirely up to you.

Import Save Files from Always Sometimes Monsters to continue your story, no matter how tragic or triumphant your ending may have been. Your entire continuity will be carried over.

Build Relationships with your spouse, friends, and more. Learn how to manage the demands of various social relationships as you maintain a life in the spotlight, and reach for your goals.

Decline Anything you don't want to do. Nearly all of the game's content is optional, including the entirety of the primary narrative. You're truly in control of the story, with a right to refusal.

Mature Content Warning
Always Sometimes Monsters deals with serious stuff, depending on your choices. Including strong language, racist, homophobic, and transphobic language, drug / alcohol use, nudity, violence, and extreme subject matter.

reviews.review:
Sometimes Always Monsters is an unconventional narrative RPG that treats ordinary adult life, relationships, personal ambition, and reputation as the foundations of its role-playing. Developed and published by Vagabond Dog, it follows a newly married author embarking on a cross-country promotional tour for an upcoming novel. What initially appears to be a promising step forward in the protagonist's career becomes considerably more complicated when accusations of plagiarism begin circulating. Instead of fighting monsters or exploring dangerous dungeons, the player must deal with rumors, friendships, marriage, professional pressures, and the consequences of their own behavior.

The journey takes place across five cities, with the protagonist meeting fans, critics, fellow travelers, and numerous other personalities along the way. Conversations are the game's primary form of interaction, but there is considerable freedom behind them. You can approach life as a dedicated professional determined to accomplish every objective, behave like an irresponsible slacker, or fall somewhere between those extremes. Countless dialogue choices help establish your personality, while everyday decisions gradually determine how other characters perceive you. The result feels closer to participating in an interactive social drama than following the traditional structure of an RPG.

One of its most distinctive features is the ability to refuse content. Many games advertise freedom while quietly forcing players toward the same major objectives, but Sometimes Always Monsters genuinely allows you to reject activities and opportunities. Even the primary narrative can largely be ignored if that is how you want to role-play your character. This freedom makes choices feel more meaningful because participation itself becomes a decision. You are not simply choosing between predetermined solutions to a problem. Sometimes you can decide that the problem is not worth your character's attention at all.

Relationships provide another important layer. Maintaining a marriage while pursuing a demanding career creates situations where professional success and personal responsibility may conflict. Friendships and interactions with your traveling companions further complicate matters. The game does not always divide decisions into obviously good and evil outcomes. Instead, many situations involve competing priorities, personal compromises, and imperfect people. Helping one person may disappoint another, while pursuing your own goals can damage relationships you previously considered important.

Returning players receive additional continuity through the ability to import a completed save from Always Sometimes Monsters. Previous decisions and outcomes can therefore influence the starting circumstances of this sequel, making it feel like a continuation of a personalized life rather than an unrelated adventure. New players can still begin without importing a save, so knowledge of the original is not an absolute requirement. However, continuing an established character gives many situations additional emotional weight because past successes, failures, and relationships already have personal history behind them.

Visually, the game uses straightforward top-down pixel graphics that emphasize function and personality rather than technical spectacle. Environments are easy to navigate and the visual approach suits its dialogue-heavy structure, although players expecting elaborate animation or highly detailed artwork may find the presentation basic. The writing carries most of the experience, so enjoyment depends heavily on whether you become invested in its characters and social situations. Its simple presentation also helps keep the focus on decisions instead of visual spectacle.

The game deals with considerably more mature material than its colorful pixel-art appearance might initially suggest. Depending on your choices, the narrative can involve mature sexual themes, LGBTQ+ relationships, alcohol and tobacco references, drug use, gambling, verbal abuse, mental-health subjects, violence, blood, and suicide. These subjects contribute to a story interested in flawed adults and uncomfortable situations rather than presenting an idealized adventure. Players sensitive to such themes should be aware that the narrative can move into emotionally difficult territory.

The biggest limitation is that the same freedom that makes the game distinctive can also produce uneven pacing. Players accustomed to combat-driven RPGs may find that long conversations and ordinary social activities lack momentum. There is no traditional battle system serving as the main attraction, and character development is primarily expressed through decisions and relationships rather than statistics, equipment, or increasingly powerful abilities. For the right audience this is precisely what makes the game fascinating, but players seeking action may struggle to remain engaged.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable rather than Verified. The game runs successfully on Steam Deck, its default controller configuration provides access to the game's functionality, and the default graphics configuration performs well. There are some compromises: certain text can appear small, and the game may display keyboard, mouse, or non-Steam Deck controller icons. External controllers can also require manually switching the active controller. These issues prevent a fully seamless handheld experience, but the game's relatively relaxed, text-focused nature still makes it reasonably well suited to portable play.

Ultimately, Sometimes Always Monsters succeeds because it understands role-playing as something broader than combat and character statistics. It asks players to construct a personality through countless small decisions and then live with the resulting relationships and consequences. Its willingness to let you refuse major content is particularly refreshing, reinforcing the idea that this is your character's life rather than a fixed story disguised as an interactive one. The modest presentation and deliberate pacing narrow its audience, but anyone who values choice-heavy storytelling, morally complicated situations, relationship management, and genuine narrative freedom should find plenty to appreciate.

Rating: 8/10
